<reason>Both sides argued with unusual sharpness and neither leaned on fake citations. A built a genuinely interesting contrarian case (concentration localizes both the mess and the enforcement tools; diffusion exports touristification into residential staircases and multiplies the households who want the tap shut), and its distinction between rationing a scarce icon and relocating complements was a real answer to B's elasticity trap. But B won the two decisive nodes. First, the seasonal half of the motion: B's pressure question forced A either to accept February spreading or deny the motion as written, and A chose the latter — declaring "a February booking is not the proposition" — which is definitional evasion of an explicit term of the resolution. B's worst-case concession ("suppose it's purely additional: the failure mode is that the city earns more and nobody is trampled") was never answered, and A's July-as-a-wall reply never engaged B's date-flexible segments. Second, "where does the next visitor go?" A answered honestly ("another city, or stay home"), which is a coherent position but hands B the cleaner comparison: A's plan protects the rest of the city by nominating one district as a permanent scrum, and A's rejoinder that those streets "are the product, not a victim" only sharpened B's sacrifice-zone frame. B also turned A's backlash argument (containment produced Venice/Amsterdam restriction) without A landing a decisive counter. A's second rebuttal being clipped for over-length is an additional execution cost at exactly the moment the weighing needed closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Q1 on seasons plus its follow-up: by isolating a February visitor who imposes near-zero crowding cost and drafts no new district, B forced A to either concede half the motion or redefine it away. A chose redefinition, and B's "the failure mode is that the city earns more and nobody is trampled" went unanswered, leaving the seasonal half of the proposition effectively uncontested on merits.</best_rebuttal>
